title: Create scripts with Kite
text:
# Create scripts with Kite

New to Kite? Read [How Kite works](How-Kite-works.html), or give your coding agent
the [agent guide](Agent-guide.html).

Start with [Your first widget](Getting-started.html). You only need Kite on your iPhone;
Xcode and a computer are not required to write scripts.

Follow [Build a daily intention widget](Progressive-tutorial.html) for five practical checkpoints.
Search [API reference](API-reference.html) for every public signature, or use
[Troubleshooting](Troubleshooting.html) when something fails.

Then use [the scripting guide](Scripting-guide.html) to add settings, saved data,
buttons, photos, Shortcuts and Control Center actions.

Ready to experiment? Copy one of these complete scripts into Kite:

| Script | What to try |
| --- | --- |
| [Daylight](examples/Daylight.tsx) | Date, progress and a native countdown. |
| [Water Garden](examples/Water%20Garden.tsx) | Persist a counter and change it with widget buttons. |
| [Quiet Frame](examples/Quiet%20Frame.tsx) | Download a photo with caching and an offline fallback. |
| [Focus Session](examples/Focus%20Session.tsx) | Start a timer from a widget or Control Center. |

The app also includes Watchlist, Habit Toggle, Next Events and Quick Note. In Scripts,
open the **+** menu and choose **Add examples** if they aren't in your library.

For precise method signatures and supported properties, use the
[API type declarations](types/index.d.ts). These describe the current
implementation. Features in the roadmap may not be available yet.

These guides cover the current Phase 1 app. Device reliability validation is still
in progress. Mac CLI/sync and Scriptable compatibility are roadmap work, not part
of these tutorials.

In builds that include offline Help, open **Help** from Settings or the editor. Help works offline. Search
finds matching sections; complete TSX examples have a **Create script from example**
action that makes an independent copy. Updates arrive with the app build.

title: How Kite works
text:
# How Kite works

Kite turns a small script into a native iPhone widget. You describe what to show,
where to place it, and what should happen when someone taps a button. Kite handles
turning that description into the widget you see on screen.

You can start from an example and change its words, colors and settings. You don't
need to build an iPhone app or connect your phone to a computer.

## From an idea to a widget

1. **Choose a starting point.** In Kite, create a Widget or Interactive widget.
   Give it a name, or keep the suggested one.
2. **Describe your content.** A script can show text, photos, progress, dates and
   data from a service. Its layout uses building blocks: a vertical stack puts
   items underneath each other; a horizontal stack puts them side by side.
3. **Try it in Kite.** Tap Run to see a preview. Change the layout or settings and
   Run again until it looks right. Errors and logs help you find problems.
4. **Add it to your Home Screen.** Add the Kite Script widget, choose a size, then
   select your script in Edit Widget. Each widget can have its own settings.
5. **Let iOS update it.** Kite prepares the content when the system requests an
   update. A refresh preference asks for updates; iOS chooses the actual timing.

[Create your first widget](Getting-started.html) walks through all five steps with
code you can copy. [Example scripts](index.html) give you a head start.

## What is inside a script?

Think of a script as a recipe with three parts:

- **Its label:** the name, supported sizes and options such as a message or a goal.
  In code, this is called `config`.
- **Its layout:** instructions for drawing the widget. For example, “show a title,
  a progress bar, and an Add button.” In code, this is `widget()`.
- **Its actions:** instructions to run after a tap, such as saving another glass
  of water. These are separate functions connected to the buttons.

Text that looks like `widget()` is a name used in code. A name on its own isn't a
complete script. The tutorials show complete files; the API reference describes
individual pieces you can use inside those files.

## Where do the numbers and images come from?

A widget can use text you enter in settings, data saved by a button, information
you allow it to read on your phone, or a request to an online service. Access to
things like Calendar needs your permission. Some services also need an API key;
keep keys in Kite's secrets settings, not in a file you share.

Kite starts a fresh run each time it needs to prepare content. To remember a
counter or completed habit, the script saves it in storage. A temporary variable
alone won't remember its value the next time the widget runs.

## Why doesn't everything update instantly?

A Home Screen widget isn't an app that runs continuously. iOS gives it short
opportunities to prepare its display so it can preserve battery life. It may show
saved content between updates. The preview is the quickest place to test edits.

Native countdown text can keep counting on screen without rerunning the script
every second. Buttons can run a short action and request updated content. Neither
mechanism makes a script a continuously running background process.

## More than Home Screen widgets

The same script can also provide a small Lock Screen view, an action that receives
input from Shortcuts, or a switch/button in Control Center. Those surfaces have
different sizes and behaviors, so test each one you plan to use. A script does not
add itself to any of these places automatically.

## Can an AI agent write the script?

Yes. Give your agent the [agent guide](Agent-guide.html) and describe what you want
it to show, which sizes you need, and where its data should come from. The guide
lists Kite's supported APIs and limits so the agent doesn't assume it is building
a web page. Review generated code before running it, especially if it uses private
data or online services. You can then paste its complete `.tsx` file into Kite.

title: Point your agent here
text:
# Point your agent here

Use this guide when asking an AI coding agent to create a Kite script. No access
to the private app repository is needed. The documentation describes the current
implementation; roadmap ideas are not available APIs.

## Give your agent this instruction

Copy this instruction and append your widget idea:

```text
Read https://juanbeniteza.github.io/kite-docs/llms-full.txt before writing code.
Create a Kite script using only the documented APIs and runtime capabilities.
Return one complete .tsx file, including config, imports and exported entry points.
Explain required permissions/secrets, supported sizes, installation and test steps.
State limitations honestly; do not invent APIs or promise exact background refreshes.
My idea: ...
```

If the agent cannot open URLs, download the plain-text guide and attach it to the
conversation. A link does not automatically give every agent browsing capability.

## Read these sources

- [How Kite works](How-Kite-works.html): a plain-language explanation for the user.
- [API reference](API-reference.html): supported arguments, properties and return types.
- [Type declarations](types/index.d.ts): the exact public contract.
- [Scripting guide](Scripting-guide.html): entry points and native services.
- [Daily Intention tutorial](Progressive-tutorial.html): a complete interactive script.
- [Water Garden](examples/Water%20Garden.tsx): persisted widget actions.
- [Quiet Frame](examples/Quiet%20Frame.tsx): native cached image loading and fallback.
- [Focus Session](examples/Focus%20Session.tsx): timelines, timer and control.

## Execution and output contract

- Deliver a single self-contained `.tsx` file by default. JavaScript/JSX is also
  supported, but TypeScript with JSX is the easiest shared format for examples.
- Use imports from `kite` and `kite/ui`. JSX creates native widget nodes; it is not
  React, HTML, CSS or a browser page. No React state/hooks, DOM, Node filesystem,
  npm package runtime, browser `fetch`, `setInterval`, or dynamic `eval`/`Function`.
  Use `http` for requests. Do not invent browser APIs from habit.
- Export `config = defineScript({...})` with a literal object. Metadata is parsed
  without executing the script. No computed fields, helper calls, spreads or
  variables inside config. Dynamic logic belongs in exported functions/helpers.
- `widget(ctx)` returns a Widget root or ascending `{ date, view }` timeline entries.
  `run()` handles app-only work/logging. `shortcut(input)` returns action output.
  `control` supplies button `press()` or toggle `get()`/`set(on)`.
- Every run starts with fresh JavaScript state. Persist JSON with `storage` and
  use `storage.update` for concurrent counters. Its callback can be retried: keep
  external side effects outside it. Dates should be saved as strings/timestamps.
- Buttons use `intent={exportedFunction}`, not a function call or inline closure.
  `params` is a JSON object passed to the handler. Widget Toggle adds `isOn` to
  that object: its handler receives `{ isOn, ...params }`. This differs from a
  Control Center toggle's `set(on)`, which receives a boolean directly.
- After a state change, return `{ reload: true }` and render the saved state again.
  Do not claim that changing a local variable updates a widget.

## Layout and system limits

- Use only the components/properties in the type declarations. Supported content
  includes stacks, grids, Text, Image, DateText, Gauge, ProgressView, Chart, Button,
  Toggle, Link, Spacer and Divider. No arbitrary HTML tags, CSS classes, web fonts,
  pixel font sizes or gradients unless an API explicitly documents them.
- Use named fonts and point-based frames. Keep layouts compact and check every
  declared family. Home Screen: small/medium/large, plus iPad extraLarge. Lock
  Screen: accessoryInline/accessoryCircular/accessoryRectangular with system
  tinting and restricted space. Don't promise a full-color Home Screen design on
  an accessory surface. Do not promise buttons in every accessory family.
- `ctx.date` is the rendering date; `ctx.displaySize` is in points, not pixels.
  Use `DateText` rather than importing `Date` and shadowing JavaScript's Date.
- iOS schedules widget runs. `refresh` is a hint, not a guaranteed interval.
  Timelines schedule display entries; they don't execute arbitrary code later.
  A native timer doesn't itself schedule notifications or trigger an action at zero.
- Keep work brief. The current normal deadline is 10 seconds with cooperative
  checks; native calls/engine built-ins aren't always interruptible. Don't add
  background loops or claim a measured memory budget that isn't documented.
- Phone compilation strips TS/JSX; it does not perform full TypeScript checking.
  Validate settings, missing storage and remote JSON at runtime. Gracefully handle
  permission denial, network failures and empty datasets.

## Native access and data

- Declare only needed permissions: network, files, calendar, reminders, location,
  notifications. Run in the app first for any required system prompts. Extensions
  cannot prompt for access. Declaration alone doesn't grant authorization.
- `storage`, `secrets`, `device` and `log` need no config permission. Secrets are
  per-script Keychain values: use `secrets.get`, not hardcoded tokens or logs.
- Use `http.image` for photos, then its returned source in Image. Native decoding
  downsizes the image; use caching and a useful offline view. Don't implement
  full-resolution image processing in JS.
- Use Kite's files API within its roots. Local files are shared with widget runs;
  iCloud file access is app-only. Do not assume arbitrary device filesystem access.
- Widget editor settings currently have four generic slots. App script settings
  expose the fuller configuration. Don't promise dynamically generated unlimited
  named system parameters or automatic placement of widgets/controls.
- Scriptable compatibility and Mac CLI/sync are roadmap work. Don't generate
  Scriptable globals, ListWidget or CLI commands as though already supported.
- Kite is for trusted scripts, not a sandbox for hostile source. Explain external
  service calls and sensitive data use. Don't embed credentials in shared output.

## Agent handoff checklist

Before handing over a script, check imports, literal config, complete exported
entry points, family layouts, persistent state, exported interaction references,
permissions and failure fallbacks. Separate APIs you verified from assumptions.
If a service contract is unknown, ask for it or clearly mark a placeholder URL;
never fabricate a working endpoint or claim testing you haven't performed.

Return installation steps: create a script, paste the complete file, Run in Kite,
configure any settings/secrets, check Preview/Logs, then add and configure Kite
Script, the Shortcuts action or the matching Kite control. Include expected output
and a repeatable tap/run test. Label preview/compiler checks separately from
physical-device checks. Don't require reinstalling the app for a script edit.

title: Your first widget
text:
# Your first widget

We'll make a small widget that shows a message, change its appearance, and put it
on your Home Screen. No web service or API key is needed.

## 1. Create a script

In Kite, go to **Scripts → + → New script**. Choose **Widget**, name it
**Hello Kite**, and tap **Create**. Leaving the name empty also works: Kite uses a
default name.

The other starters are useful later: **Interactive widget** adds working buttons,
**Shortcuts action** processes input, and **Control** creates a Control Center
switch or button. A script can support several of these surfaces at once.

## 2. Replace the code

Select the existing code in the editor and paste this whole example:

```tsx
import type { WidgetContext } from "kite";
import { Widget, VStack, Text, Image } from "kite/ui";

export const config = defineScript({
  name: "Hello Kite",
  icon: { symbol: "sun.max.fill", color: "#72DCC5" },
  widget: { families: ["small", "medium"], refresh: "hourly" },
  settings: {
    message: { type: "text", title: "Message", default: "Made on my iPhone." },
  },
});

export async function widget(ctx: WidgetContext) {
  return (
    <Widget background="#0D1C2C">
      <VStack align="leading" spacing={8}>
        <Image symbol="sun.max.fill" font="title2" color="#72DCC5" />
        <Text font="headline" color="#FFFFFF">Hello, Kite</Text>
        <Text font="caption" color="#72DCC5">
          {String(ctx.settings.message ?? "Made on my iPhone.")}
        </Text>
      </VStack>
    </Widget>
  );
}
```

This is TypeScript with JSX, saved as a `.tsx` file. JSX is the tag-shaped part of
the code, such as `<Text>`. It describes the widget layout; it isn't HTML.
You don't need React or a build step. Kite compiles the file on your phone.

## 3. Run it

Tap **Run**. While editing, Run is available in the row above the keyboard; the
keyboard button dismisses it. With the keyboard hidden, Run is at the bottom.
Kite saves the latest code before running it.

You should see a dark widget with a mint sun and your message in **Preview**.
Try the small and medium preview sizes. **Logs** shows messages from `console.log`.
If compilation fails, Kite stays in **Code** and shows the error and line number.

Change `Hello, Kite` to your own heading, then Run again. Change `#0D1C2C` to
`#243B35` to change the background. Keep the quotation marks around both values.

## 4. Understand the pieces

- `import` brings in the Kite components and types used by this file.
- `config` describes the script: its name, sizes and settings. Kite reads this
  without executing the script. Keep it a plain object of literal values.
- `widget(ctx)` builds the view. `ctx` contains the selected size, settings and date.
- `Widget` is the root. `VStack` arranges children vertically; `HStack` is horizontal.
- `Text` draws text, and `Image symbol` draws an SF Symbol.
- `{...}` inside JSX evaluates a JavaScript expression.

Changing `config.icon` changes the script's library icon. The widget's sun comes
from the separate `<Image>` line.

## 5. Change a setting

Open the editor's settings button and change **Message**. Run again to see it.
Settings let you customize a script without editing the source every time.

## 6. Add it to the Home Screen

1. Touch and hold an empty area of the Home Screen and open the widget picker.
2. Find Kite and add **Kite Script** in small or medium size.
3. Touch and hold the new widget, choose **Edit Widget**, and choose **Hello Kite**.
4. Set its options if offered, then close the editor.

Kite must compile your script in the app first. After changing code, open Kite and
Run again before checking the Home Screen. iOS schedules widget updates;
`refresh: "hourly"` is a request, not an exact hourly timer.

## Import a complete script instead

Open a linked `.tsx` example from [the docs index](index.html), copy all its code,
create a script in Kite and replace the starter's contents. Keep the whole file,
including imports and `config`.

You can also copy a `.tsx` file into the folder shown under **Kite → Settings →
Script library**, then refresh Scripts. Use that displayed location: it may be
in iCloud Drive or in the local Files app folder. Never put API keys in shared files.

## If something goes wrong

| What you see | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Red error with a line number | Check that line for missing brackets, commas or quotes. Copy the complete example again if needed. |
| A JSX parsing error | Make sure the file uses `.tsx` or `.jsx`, not plain `.ts`. |
| Script missing from the widget picker | Open Kite and Run first; check that `widget` is exported and the chosen size is in `config.widget.families`. |
| Run succeeds but nothing visible changes | `run()` may only log. A widget needs `widget()`; changing data may require a button press. Check Logs and Preview. |
| Old Home Screen content | Run in Kite, check widget configuration, then allow iOS to request its update. Preview is the fastest edit/test loop. |
| Permission failure | Declare the permission in `config`, then run in Kite to grant any required system access. Widgets cannot show permission prompts. |

Next: [save data, add buttons and use native APIs](Scripting-guide.html).

title: Build a daily intention widget
Scripting guide
text:
# Scripting guide

[Start with a complete first widget](Getting-started.html) if you're new to Kite.
Each code block below is a separate, complete script unless described otherwise.

## How a script runs

Kite calls exported entry points for the surface you're using:

| Export | Called for | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `widget(ctx)` | Widget rendering and preview | A `Widget` tree or dated timeline entries |
| `run()` | App execution for a run-only script | Work and console output |
| `shortcut(input)` | A Shortcuts action | Text, JSON, number or a supported file result |
| `control` | Control Center button or switch | `press()`, or `get()` and `set(on)` |
| Other exported functions | Widget Button/Toggle handlers | Usually `{ reload: true }` |

Run in the editor builds the script and tests its available surface; a control's
Preview has Press or switch controls. Defining a function doesn't execute its body.
For example, Focus Session starts when you press Start, not simply when you open it.

Each execution gets a fresh JavaScript context. A normal variable doesn't persist
between executions. Use `storage` for saved state shared by the same script's
app, widget and control runs. Different scripts have separate storage.

## Save data and add a button

This counter is a complete interactive widget. Tap **Add** in Preview or on the
Home Screen; the number should survive another Run.

```tsx
import { storage } from "kite";
import { Widget, VStack, Text, Button } from "kite/ui";

export const config = defineScript({
  name: "My Counter",
  widget: { families: ["small", "medium"], refresh: "daily" },
});

export async function increment() {
  await storage.update<number>("count", old => (old ?? 0) + 1);
  return { reload: true };
}

export async function widget() {
  const count = await storage.get<number>("count") ?? 0;
  return <Widget><VStack spacing={8}>
    <Text font="largeTitle" weight="bold">{count}</Text>
    <Button intent={increment} label="Add" symbol="plus.circle.fill" />
  </VStack></Widget>;
}
```

Use the exported function reference `intent={increment}`, not `increment()`.
The latter would call it while building the view. For parameters, pass a JSON
object through the Button's `params` property and accept it in your handler.
Prefer `storage.update` for counters so simultaneous actions don't overwrite
one another. `get`, `set`, `remove` and `keys` are also available. Store JSON values,
not functions or Date objects; store a date as an ISO string or timestamp.

## Layout and size

`Widget` contains `VStack`, `HStack` and `ZStack` containers. Use `Spacer`, `Divider`,
`Text`, `Image`, `DateText`, `Gauge`, `ProgressView`, `Chart`, `Button`, `Toggle`
and `Link` inside them. These render as native SwiftUI; CSS and HTML aren't supported.

Common properties include `padding`, `background`, `cornerRadius`, `opacity` and
`frame`. Text supports named fonts such as `headline`, `caption` and `largeTitle`,
plus `weight`, `color` and `lineLimit`. Sizes are in points.

Use `ctx.family` to show less content in `small` than in `large`. Home Screen
families are `small`, `medium`, `large` and iPad `extraLarge`. Lock Screen families
are `accessoryInline`, `accessoryCircular` and `accessoryRectangular`. Keep accessory
layouts simple: they use system tinting and have very little space. Choose a
supported family in `config.widget.families` and check it in Preview.

See [Daylight](examples/Daylight.tsx) for responsive layouts and progress.

## Settings and secrets

Declare settings as literal objects in `config.settings`, then read values through
`ctx.settings` in `widget`. Types are `text`, `number`, `toggle`, `enum`, `color` and
`secret`. Use defaults and validate values before calculations. The first-widget
tutorial demonstrates a text setting.

The current Home Screen widget editor has four generic setting slots. It can't
create unlimited named system fields from your source. Use Kite's script settings
for the full editor. Secret values belong in the app's secrets settings/Keychain;
read them with `await secrets.get("apiKey")` from `kite`. Don't hardcode keys in
source or log them.

`config` cannot depend on variables, function calls, spread expressions or computed
values. For instance, put `"My Widget"` directly in `config.name`, rather than a
variable containing that string. Ordinary dynamic logic belongs in functions.

## Network requests and photos

Declare `permissions: ["network"]` in `config`. Import `http` from `kite`.
`await http.json(url, { cache: "15m" })` downloads parsed JSON. With
`http.fetch`, check `response.ok` before reading `response.json()` or `text()`.
Handle errors and missing response fields so the widget still has useful content.

For images, use `await http.image(url, { cache: "1d" })`, then put the returned
source into `<Image src={source} />`. Kite downsizes images natively; don't download
full images as raw data just to resize them in JavaScript. `maxPixelSize` optionally
sets the longest edge in pixels.

[Quiet Frame](examples/Quiet%20Frame.tsx) is a complete downloadable photo widget
with a fallback. It needs internet access on the first load, but no API key.

## Permissions and native services

| Module imported from `kite` | Permission in `config.permissions` | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `http` | `network` | Requests, JSON and cached images |
| `files` | `files` | Read/write text files |
| `calendar` | `calendar` | Read calendars and create events |
| `reminders` | `reminders` | Read, create and complete reminders |
| `location` | `location` | Coordinates and geocoding |
| `notify` | `notifications` | Schedule/cancel notifications |
| `storage`, `secrets`, `device`, `log` | No declared permission | Saved JSON, Keychain, device info and logging |

Run permission-using scripts in Kite first. Only the app can present system
permission dialogs. A declaration alone doesn't grant system access. Keep background
work brief and handle denied access. iCloud file access is app-only; local script
files use shared storage available to widgets. Never assume arbitrary filesystem
access. See [the declarations](types/index.d.ts) for each method's arguments.

## Shortcuts

Create a **Shortcuts action** starter, or paste this script:

```tsx
export const config = defineScript({ name: "Uppercase Text" });

export async function shortcut(input: unknown) {
  const text = input == null ? "" : String(input);
  return text.toUpperCase();
}
```

Run it in Kite first. In Apple's Shortcuts app, create a shortcut, search for Kite,
add its run-script action, select **Uppercase Text**, and supply text as the input.
Add Show Result after it. With input `hello`, the result should be `HELLO`.
Kite provides separate actions for general text/JSON, number and file results;
choose the one matching your return value. This example uses text/JSON. Device
validation of the full Shortcuts UI flow is still pending.

## Control Center

This is a complete persisted switch. It doesn't require a widget:

```tsx
import { storage } from "kite";
import type { Control } from "kite";

export const config = defineScript({ name: "My Switch" });

export const control: Control = {
  kind: "toggle",
  title: "My Switch",
  symbol: "bolt.fill",
  async get() { return await storage.get<boolean>("on") ?? false; },
  async set(on: boolean) {
    await storage.set("on", on);
    return { reload: true };
  },
};
```

Run it and test the switch in Preview. Then edit Control Center, add **Kite Toggle**,
and choose **My Switch** in its configuration. It saves a boolean; it doesn't
operate a light or device until you add that integration yourself.

For a momentary action, use `kind: "button"` with `async press()` and add
**Kite Button** instead. [Focus Session](examples/Focus%20Session.tsx) combines a
button control, widget and shared storage in one script.

## Dates, countdowns and refreshes

Use `ctx.date` as the rendering date. `DateText` with `style="timer"` displays a
native relative timer; it doesn't require rerunning your script every second.
Return an array of `{ date, view }` entries to schedule different views for future
times, in ascending order. Daylight and Focus Session demonstrate this.

`refresh` hints include `"15m"`, `"30m"`, `"hourly"`, `"daily"` and `"never"`.
iOS controls actual widget execution. Don't use a JavaScript loop or `setInterval`
to keep a widget alive. Timers don't extend Kite's run deadline, and a displayed
countdown alone doesn't schedule a notification or execute a function when it ends.

## Runtime boundaries

Use `kite` modules rather than browser or Node APIs: there is no DOM, React runtime,
Node filesystem or Node package loader. TypeScript annotations are stripped on the
phone; the phone doesn't perform a full TypeScript typecheck. Dynamic code such as
`eval` and `new Function` is blocked. Deadline checks are cooperative; Kite is not a
security sandbox for hostile source. Read scripts before importing them.

To debug, add `console.log("count", count)`, Run, and open Logs. Avoid logging secrets
or personal data. Keep functions small and test changes in Preview before checking
the system widget. Share the `.tsx` file, with keys removed, through Files or a link.

title: API reference
Troubleshooting
text:
# Troubleshooting

Use this order: save and Run in Kite → read the first error → check Preview → test
the actual widget, shortcut or control. Fix one thing at a time. Logs can contain
personal information; remove tokens and private data before sharing them.

## Compile errors

**Unexpected token / JSX parse error:** confirm the filename ends in `.tsx` or
`.jsx` when it contains tags. Check matching braces, parentheses, quotes and closing
tags. The reported position may follow the real mistake, so check the previous line.
Smart quotes pasted from prose can break JavaScript. Copy examples from code blocks.

**Invalid config / metadata error:** config is read without running source. Write
literal strings, numbers, booleans, arrays and plain objects. Don't compute a name,
spread another object into config, or call helpers there. Put logic in functions.

**Import/module/export error:** use supported `kite` and `kite/ui` imports. Node,
browser and arbitrary npm dependencies aren't available. Check spelling and export
`widget`, `shortcut`, `control` or `run`. Relative modules require their files to be
present in the library; start with one complete file when diagnosing imports.

## Runtime errors

**Undefined / cannot read property:** inspect the value before accessing a field.
A setting may be absent, storage may have no value, and a network response may not
match your assumed shape. Use defaults and validate untrusted JSON. Phone compilation
strips types; it doesn't prove that external data matches a TypeScript annotation.

**Timeout:** remove endless loops and unnecessary work. Cache requests and reduce
large inputs. Don't try to keep a script running to animate a widget. A deadline is
cooperative; it doesn't make every native call or engine built-in interruptible.

**Invalid result:** widget must return a Widget tree or dated entries containing
`date` and `view`. Don't return raw strings, Promises you forgot to await inside
data, or circular JavaScript objects. See the first-widget example.

## Requests and permissions

**Permission denied / undeclared permission:** add the relevant literal permission
in config, then Run in the app. Widgets and controls cannot present authorization
prompts. If you already denied system access, review Kite in iOS Settings. Return
safe fallback content when permission stays denied. Network declaration is required
but doesn't itself grant access to calendar, location or other protected data.

**HTTP failure:** check status with `http.fetch` and verify the URL, authentication,
service response and connectivity. Log a status or a redacted summary, not an API
key or the full private response. Cache can serve old content; shorten the cache
window while diagnosing, then restore a reasonable window. API keys belong in secrets.

**Photo blank:** load through `http.image`, pass the returned source to Image, and
provide an aspect and useful space in the layout. Run online in the app first.
Handle download failure with text or an SF Symbol. Don't assume a remote URL is a
local cached image source. Quiet Frame is a working reference.

## Widget problems

**Script absent:** Run in Kite and resolve compile errors first. Export widget and
declare the family you're adding. Pick Kite Script, not an internal benchmark widget.
Refresh the library after copying a file through Files.

**Preview works, Home Screen is stale or blank:** verify the widget's selected script
and setting slots, Run again in Kite, and wait for the system's reload. Refresh is a
hint. Preview and real widgets have different execution environments and budgets.
A prior failure can leave the last good render visible. Inspect logs/Diagnostics for
that surface before assuming your latest edit ran. Record the time, script, size,
iOS version and screenshot if the problem persists.

**Button does nothing:** pass an exported function reference to intent, not a call.
Save state with storage, return `{ reload: true }`, and render the state again.
A value held only in a module variable disappears after execution. Keep handler
parameters JSON-compatible. Test Preview and Home Screen separately.

**Lock Screen looks different:** accessory widgets use system tinting and small
layouts. Background colors and full Home Screen compositions won't transfer directly.
Test the exact accessory family and reduce content.

## Shortcuts and controls

**No shortcut output:** export shortcut(input), supply input in the Shortcuts action,
and choose the action matching text/JSON, number or file output. A console log isn't
the returned result. Check Preview output first, then Show Result in Shortcuts.

**Control missing:** export a control with kind toggle or button. Run in Kite, then
add the corresponding Kite Toggle or Kite Button and choose the script. Merely
exporting control doesn't add it to Control Center automatically.

**Control resets:** implement get() using persistent storage, and write the same
key in set(on). A control with a boolean variable at file scope loses it each run.

## Recovery without losing scripts

Copy the script file somewhere safe before large edits. Removing a Home Screen
widget doesn't fix source errors. Avoid reinstalling Kite as an initial debugging
step: local files and state may be lost. Keep a backup and use a fresh copy of the
smallest example to separate source problems from environment problems.

For a useful bug report include: the smallest script that reproduces it (secrets
removed), what you expected, what happened, family/surface, app build, iOS version,
and relevant redacted logs. Device benchmark CSV is useful for the three-day
reliability test, but isn't required for an ordinary syntax question.
